wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, left and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Sustained 5.11 climbing and serious exposure on the steep face
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms; Core Zone camping needs a permit
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.baseFinding:
Go to the outside corner and start just right of it. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the right of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

That corner is the anchor for the whole left end of the face, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

The honest warning about where this route ends, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the west ridge, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

Sequence check: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach: about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain on the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Cross-country travel past the upper lakes to the base of the south face
Sustained 5.11 climbing and serious exposure on the steep face
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Afternoon thunderstorms

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: terrain to climber's right cliffs out, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet. It is also the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed. Some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.
hazards: Long approach: about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain on the Snow Lakes trail to Lake Viviane
Faint, easily lost path over granite up to Gnome Tarn and the base
Loose rock near the chockstone tunnel and runout sections on the upper flare and chimney pitches
North-side rappels on climber-built slung anchors; bring cordage; the line backs up when busy
Afternoon thunderstorms and party traffic on a very popular line

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay climber's left (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east through the Core's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right toward the waterfalls cliffs out and has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of the pass, worse in afternoon heat
Misleading, multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
Descent is rappels, not a walk-off; very long day with the descent often in the dark
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do not go over the first bump in front of you — go around it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge balanced, dish-shaped rock — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an overhanging rock at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a wide crack, about 5.6, in a conspicuously white section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice; uncontrolled slide risk on the pass, up or down
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
Early-season snow and ice on approach ledges
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go around the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments to Prusik Pass

bivy.name: Inspiration and Perfection Lakes
bivy.notes: The most used camping ground in the basin, on the benches and the bluff between the two lakes, and the closest general camp to the peak — the signed path toward Prusik Pass leaves the western shore of Perfection Lake. Open granite and heather, thoroughly worn in, and shared with mountain goats that come in for salt. The exposed benches right at Isolation and Tranquil Lakes are above treeline and windy by comparison.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October, and Prusik's camps lie in the Core Enchantment Zone, which is allocated by lottery. Maximum group size is eight. Camp only on ground already worn bare — do not clear vegetation, move rocks or build walls. Fires are prohibited anywhere above 5,000 ft or within half a mile of a lake, which rules them out at every camp in this basin; solid-fuel and wood-burning stoves are also prohibited above 5,000 ft, but liquid and canister gas stoves are allowed. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area, and no stock is allowed in the Core Zone. Maximum stay is fourteen consecutive days. Two traps worth knowing: a Snow Zone permit lets you climb here for the day but you must camp at or below Upper Snow Lake, and a Colchuck Zone permit does not allow camping above the 6,500 ft contour below Aasgard Pass. A Core Zone permit, by contrast, allows camping in any of the five zones on the way in or out.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count for any site in the basin. The permit is the real constraint: the Core Zone quota counts people entering per day rather than groups, and the whole of a permitted group must camp together at one site.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to the Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass area below the peak. More gain than Aasgard Pass but no steep snow or talus headwall.
hazards: Long approach past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass, with more gain than Aasgard
Unprotected 5.7 friction slab crux and loose blocks on the lower ridge
Exposed traverse before the crux
Afternoon thunderstorms with limited retreat; rockfall from parties above
Descent is rappels on tat and rings, not a walk-off

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
camps: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.
hazards: Brush-choked valley approaches and heavy blowdown, thousands of downed logs on the Middle Fork valley
Faint or obscured tread near the Eureka Creek turn
Creek fords that can run high in early season
Short exposed scrambling on the connecting ridge to the south; loose rock on the ridge crest
Sheer north face immediately off the summit; stay on the south side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue
wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the Hidden Lakes

approachLogistics.trailhead: Billy Goat Trailhead (end of Eightmile Creek Road)

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.
hazards: Rough, brushy cross-country of two to three miles beyond Ptarmigan Creek to reach the base
Long trail approach from below 3,500 ft with little maintenance
Loose talus and scree underfoot on the summit slopes
Sheer north face; stay on the south and southeast side
Afternoon thunderstorms; extreme remoteness with no fast rescue

wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs about four miles and roughly two thousand one hundred feet to Lower Crater Lake; the upper lake lies off to the south-south-west and is not on the way. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.baseFinding:
The route leaves the trail at the lake - there is no tread beyond it. From the lake basin the south-east ridge rises to the north-west toward a col at about 8,000 ft. The ridge is the route and the test is symmetry: once established you should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

If the ground closes in and you are climbing a confined, extremely loose chute, you have slipped off the crest onto a flanking gully. Those gullies are the other route's ground, gained from the next drainage north, and they are notably worse rock than the crest.

At the col near 8,000 ft the summit is along the crest, not directly above. A small separate peak stands west of the ridge saddle and is routinely mistaken for the top; the true high point is the eastern one and reaching it is a tedious traverse over talus and large boulders past several intervening bumps.

So the confirmation is effort, not elevation: if you arrived at a summit within a few minutes of gaining the crest and did not cross bouldery bumps to get there, you are on the wrong high point and should look east along the ridge.

wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side
wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la.baseFinding:
From the lake the crest is gained by a loose gully, and the gully is unpleasant enough that its quality is the confirmation. Parties commonly exit it about half-way up onto the parallel rib, which holds more solid rock, and return to it higher; the rib is a refuge beside the gully rather than a separate line, so keep the gully in sight.

If the chute you are in is solid and enjoyable, it is probably not the one - several chutes rise out of this basin and the route's own is notorious.

At the top the saddle is on the crest, and the summit is east of it. A small peak stands just west of the saddle; a summit reached in a few minutes by turning left out of the gully is that lower point, not the top.

The true high point costs a traverse over talus and large boulders past intervening bumps. Arriving without that traverse means you are in the wrong place. Coming from this side the ridge is joined further west than the south-east ridge joins it, which is exactly why this mistake is easier to make on this approach than on the other one.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.baseFinding:
The gully above the lake is the route and it is the worst ground of the day - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the rib that parallels it, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

If the ground you are climbing is pleasant, you are not in the right gully. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

The critical negative marker is on the ridge, not on the approach: a small peak stands just west of the saddle, and it is not the summit. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble eastward along the ridge. If you topped out of the gully and went left to a summit within a few minutes, you are on the lower point west of the saddle.

The positive test at the top is the walk. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit
wa_raven_ridge_standard_route.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is where the maintained trail ends at the lake and the ridge above it begins. The south-east ridge rises from the lake basin toward a col at about 8,000 ft - the ridge is the handrail and it should have ground falling away on both sides once you are established on it.

If you find yourself in a confined, very loose chute, you have dropped off the crest into one of the gullies on its flank. That is the other route's ground, approached from the other drainage, and it is not where this line goes.

At the col, the summit is the high point along the crest and it is not the first bump. The ridge here carries several intervening high points, and a small peak stands west of the ridge saddle that is regularly mistaken for the top. The true summit is the eastern high point; if you have gone west from a saddle and arrived quickly, you are on the wrong one.

The practical cross-check is talus. Reaching the true summit involves a tedious out-and-back over talus and large boulders rather than a quick step up from wherever you gained the crest.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Andrews Creek to Remmel Lake
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: The shortest line to the peak. Walk the Andrews Creek trail up the valley past the Meadow Lake and Peepsight junctions, then continue to Remmel Lake at the foot of the northwest ridge. The lower valley is burned and can hold a lot of blowdown.
hazards: Burned lower Andrews Creek valley can hold a lot of blowdown
Off-trail bushwhack from Remmel Lake through boggy, mosquito-heavy forest to the treeline camp
Remote, seldom-visited technical terrain far from help, with no cell coverage
Exposed rappels on the west side of the gendarmes
Loose, exposed granite on the upper ridge and exposed gendarme scrambling
Lightning exposure on the summit area
Steep scree and loose boulders on the west-slope descent

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. It is also the piece of this zone most likely to be open. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: A longer but gentler and generally better-kept trail. From the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road, follow the Chewuch River trail north toward Four Point Lake and on to Remmel Lake. Most parties break the walk with a night along the river.
hazards: Long walk-in along the Chewuch River trail; most parties spend a night on the way
Off-trail bushwhack from Remmel Lake through boggy, mosquito-heavy forest to the treeline camp
Remote, seldom-visited technical terrain far from help, with no cell coverage
Exposed rappels on the west side of the gendarmes
Loose, exposed granite on the upper ridge and exposed gendarme scrambling
Lightning exposure on the summit area
Steep scree and loose boulders on the west-slope descent

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: About two miles of intermittent bushwhack above the confluence through slide alder and downed timber, with a boot path that comes and goes
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower unmaintained trail
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid. It can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, and it joins the same finish as the Reynolds Creek way.
hazards: Longer day with big elevation gain via Williams Lake and over Williams Butte and War Creek Ridge
Drop through a cliff-band boulder break into the upper South Fork basin; route-finding needed
Avalanche terrain on the summit gully whenever it holds snow
Loose rock and talus on the upper gully and Class 3-4 summit block
Lingering snow in the summit gully through early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak

wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.hours: 4-5 to camp, about 2 more to the summit
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.baseFinding:
The climbing is the summit pyramid above the glacier, and the mistake to avoid is attacking it straight on.

From the top of the glacier you arrive under the southwest side of the summit block. Do not start up the steepest ground directly in front of you. Trend up and right to a flat ledge just below the top; the finish is a short chimney-like feature on the south side of the pyramid. You should find yourself on a system of solid but increasingly exposed class 3 ledges, not on a face.

The last confirmation is a short class 4 move — about twenty feet of it, one awkward crack or chimney-like exit that puts you through a notch in the summit rocks onto the top. There is a fixed rappel station at that spot, and finding a fixed anchor is the clearest proof from the ground that you are on the standard line and not a variation.

The trap is the dihedral. Left of the standard notch there is a steeper dihedral feature that reads as the obvious line; it goes at fourth to low fifth class on loose rock and wants gear. If you are looking at a clean-cut corner rather than a rubble ledge that leads around and right, you are on the harder variation.

In poor visibility: the block is small and unmistakable once you are at it, so the navigation problem is the glacier, not the rock. Late season the glacier surface is cut by meltwater runnels that look like crevasses and crevasses that look like runnels — parties report going up and climber's right, climbing diagonally across the gullies, because that side reads more reliably.

wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.name: Car-to-car day push
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier.baseFinding: Identical to the camp version — the pyramid above the top of the Sahale Glacier, gained by trending right to the ledge below the top and the short chimney-like exit on the south side at the fixed rappel station.

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
camps: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
hazards: Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed; rope up and carry a rescue kit
Red Ledge is serious when banked with snow, common into early July
Cornices near Cache Col and approach ridgelines, worst in early season
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.baseFinding: The Le Conte-Sentinel col is the reference: a flat notch at the top of the glacier carrying dry gravel bivy platforms, the only level dry ground for a long way in any direction. From the notch the peak's west side presents one continuous basin of snow running up to a rock face, and that snow is the route. Its top is the only place on the face where a broad, walkable ledge cuts leftward, to the north, beneath a short cliff band. Those two features together are the proof: continuous snow steepening as it rises, and an obvious ledge running left off the top of it. If the snow you have chosen tops out against blank rock with no ledge leading off it, you are too far south in the basin. If you are on bare rock with no snow beneath you at all, you have wandered onto the east side, which degrades into rotten rock and steep snow — that is the side parties get wrong on the descent, and it is not the route.

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.name: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The camp at the south end of the high traverse, under the Dana and Chickamin glaciers. Sentinel and Old Guard are climbed from here or from the col above.
bivy.capacity: Several sites on slabs and heather near the lakes

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: Say it plainly: these are not sites, they are wherever a party gets to. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Downey Creek Trailhead (Trail #768, Suiattle River Road)

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, walk the Downey Creek trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge, then cross the Dana Glacier country to White Rock Lakes. From the lakes, work back up onto the South Cascade Glacier to reach the peak. Plan on several days of off-trail and glacier travel.
hazards: Several days of off-trail and glacier travel from Downey Creek via the brushy Bachelor Creek path, Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge
Crevasses on the Dana and South Cascade Glaciers
Whiteout route-finding across glaciated basins
Short low-5th-class rock step above the snow ramp on the west ridge; can be wet or icy
Extreme remoteness: no cell coverage, long self-rescue times

wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.hours: 2.5-3 to camp, about 2.5 more to the notch
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
hazards: Wrong-gully error — the defining hazard of this approach, with a fatal precedent
Bergschrund or seracs barring the direct gully entry
Rockfall in the gully, natural and from parties above
Poor natural anchors — a boulder anchor failure caused the 2005 fatalities
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe traverse
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.baseFinding:
This is the most consequential base-finding problem on this list, and it has killed people.

The correct line: from a position on the glacier directly below the tower — not past it — a single gully breaks through the steep rock band. Follow it up to a snow patch or sloping terrace at the base of the tower. From that terrace, a short second gully leads to a notch, and the notch is the start of the Southeast Ridge. Some parties also describe a snow gully west of the tower that gives access to that same wide bench below the objective.

The test to apply before committing: does this gully put me on a terrace directly under the fin? If you are climbing a gully that trends away from being underneath the tower, you are in the wrong one. Being on rock is not evidence of being on route — there are similar-looking gullies here.

On 10 July 2005 a six-person party crossed the glacier, walked past the standard access gully and climbed a similar-looking gully further along. The traverse back toward the correct line put them under rockfall, which struck a climber; during the retreat rappel a natural boulder anchor failed. Three died and a fourth was seriously injured. Every subsequent description of this approach leads with the same instruction: identify the correct gully.

Carry a beta photo or a GPS track. In cloud, when you cannot see the fin above you, this approach should not be committed to on guesswork.

wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
hazards: Wrong-gully error, harder to rule out once the snow has gone
Loose scree and climber-triggered rockfall in the gully
Open moat at the glacier-rock junction
Rockfall from parties rappelling the descent line
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge.baseFinding:
The identification rule does not change: the correct gully is the one directly beneath the tower that delivers you onto the sloping terrace at the fin's base, followed by a short gully to the notch that begins the Southeast Ridge.

Late season it is arguably harder to be sure, because the snow that made the gully obvious from a distance has gone and several dry rubble chutes look alike from the glacier. Rely on the view from lower down: the gully, terrace and notch are all visible from the approach trail and from camp, so fix the line in your head before you lose the perspective.

Descent parties commonly rappel part of the route and then off rock to the west of the approach gully, so a fixed station west of your gully is a supporting sign you are in the right corridor — but it is a weaker signal than the terrace itself.

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more
wa_silver_star_glacier.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the far side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy ramp about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
wa_silver_star_glacier.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
wa_silver_star_glacier.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.
